transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-03-10 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alice Morgan (Redwood AE), Ben Cho (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (BlueWave CTO), Maria Lopez (Eng Manager), Tom Nguyen (ML Eng)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
Redwood walked BlueWave through the Hosted API chat basics: streaming behavior, key generation params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry and fallback patterns. Customer is evaluating hosted pilot vs dedicated capacity for a clinical triage assistant; main constraints are 95th-percentile latency target ~200ms, PHI handling concerns, and predictable cost. Action items: send pricing, run a small benchmark with customer's prompt set, share SOC2/security docs and an infra diagram.

Topics (auto, may be incomplete):
- Streaming chunking & reconnect behavior
- Retry/backoff patterns and idempotency tokens
- Parameter tuning for temperature/top_p/max_new_tokens
- Fallback model variants and prefix/KV caching
- Console demo: request traces and token cost breakdown
- Security/compliance: SOC2, data retention, KMS

Questions (raised during call):
- How does streaming handle partial responses on disconnect?
- If a request fails mid-stream, can we resume without repeating tokens?
- What are typical latency vs cost tradeoffs for short-chat workloads?

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alice Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alice from Redwood, AE. We've got Ben on the line, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Raj Patel: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited.
[00:09] Maria Lopez: Hi, yeah thanks for doing this. We wanted to focus on streaming behavior and what happens in failure cases.
[00:15] Ben Cho: Great, that's what we'll demo. Quick agenda: live quickstart to the Hosted Chat endpoint, show streaming chunks, then talk tuning parameters (temp/top-p/max tokens), then retries and fallback patterns.
[00:25] Tom Nguyen: Also curious about KV cache, you mentioned prefix caching on the docs.
[00:28] Ben Cho: Yep, we'll cover that. Quick qualification: Raj, you mentioned clinical triage assistant — are you planning to pass PHI to Redwood hosted API or do you want a VPC/private deployment?
[00:38] Raj Patel: We're starting with limited PHI, but for pilot we can anonymize. Long-term we probably need private deployment, but for now we want a hosted POC to iterate fast. Latency SLO is 200ms p95, and throughput is around 80 reqs/sec during business hours.
[00:54] Alice Morgan: That's helpful. Hosted can absolutely support low-latency cases, and we can show how batching and continuous KV cache help cost without violating latencies. For 80 rps we'd likely recommend a dedicated pool if you want steady per-token unit economics, but hosted pilot is typical.
[01:12] Maria Lopez: What's the expected token cost for short prompts? Most of our chats are 30-120 tokens generated.
[01:20] Ben Cho: For short-gen workloads, cost is dominated by per-request overhead unless you enable prefix caching and small model variants. We'll show token breakdown in Console.
[01:28] Raj Patel: Ok, demo time.
[01:35] Ben Cho: I'm going to share my screen and run a curl against the Hosted Chat endpoint. Note: sample code in the docs shows streaming via SSE/websocket depending on SDK.
[01:45] [screen share noise]
[02:00] Ben Cho: Here I'm sending a chat request with stream=true, temperature=0.2, max_new_tokens=80. You'll see the response in chunks.
[02:12] Ben Cho (typing): curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat 
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>" 
  -d '{"stream":true, "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"I have a sore throat, what should I do?"}], "model":"redwood-chat-medium"}'
[02:38] [00:02:38] Response chunk: "token1 token2..." (Ben narrating)
[02:45] Maria Lopez: Hmm, the chunks look small, does that increase latency?
[02:48] Ben Cho: Good q. Chunks are emitted as the model generates. There's a tradeoff: more frequent smaller chunks improves perceived interactivity but increases network overhead. You can tune server-side chunking thresholds and client-side buffering.
[03:00] Raj Patel: If the client disconnects halfway, can the request be resumed?
[03:05] Ben Cho: Short answer: not exactly resumable token-by-token in the Hosted product right now. You can design idempotency + retry logic: send the same request with an idempotency key and the service will generally provide a consistent fresh completion or fall back to a cached prefix result. For long responses we recommend checkpointing at application-level or using the KV cache to store prefix state, then re-hydrate on retry. There's a known limitation with partial stream resume; we're working on a resume feature for long-running streams.
[03:36] Tom Nguyen: So if we retry will we get duplicates and double bill for repeated tokens?
[03:40] Ben Cho: Retries can incur duplicate tokens unless you use the console's suggested retry patterns. For example, short timeouts -> exponential backoff with monotonic idempotency keys; Redwood will detect duplicate idempotency keys within a window and avoid double-processing in many cases. But for streamed chunks mid-response it's safer to re-ask only the missing tail and stitch responses client-side.
[03:58] Maria Lopez: Can you show the Console tracing so we can see token cost and latency per request?
[04:05] Ben Cho: Yep. Switching to Console. 
[04:12] [screen share noise]
[04:20] Ben Cho: Here's a per-request trace: you can see request timestamp, model variant, tokens in/out, cost estimate, and latency histogram. We also surface routing (hosted vs dedicated) and whether prefix cache hit occurred.
[04:38] Raj Patel: That prefix cache hit — what's the cache key? Is it exact-match on prompt prefix?
[04:43] Ben Cho: It can be configured. Default is a rolling prefix of recent conversation history tokens and some normalized prompt identifiers. In practice, you can enable semantic prefix caching: we hash canonicalized prompts to match common queries. Note: docs sometimes say KV cash — in voice it sounded like cash, but it's KV cache.
[05:10] Maria Lopez: Security question: if we use hosted, how long is the prompt retained? We need to ensure we meet PHI retention rules.
[05:18] Alice Morgan: Good point. Hosted default retention is 30 days for logs, but you can opt into no-retention for prompt/response storage or a shorter window. For PHI we usually recommend Private (VPC) or Dedicated with a HIPAA BA if you need long-term compliance. We'll send SOC2 and our infra diagram in the follow-up.
[05:36] Raj Patel: Cool. Back to streaming — what about backpressure? If we flood with bursts, will Redwood throttle?
[05:44] Ben Cho: We have rate limiting and per-tenant burst protection. On hosted, if you exceed your quota, you'll get 429s; best practice is token bucket on the client and exponential backoff. For Dedicated you can set autoscaling policies and burst capacity.
[06:00] Tom Nguyen: You mentioned model variants — what do we pick for accuracy vs latency?
[06:05] Ben Cho: Typical pattern: use redwood-chat-small or medium for latency-sensitive, low-cost paths, and redwood-chat-large for higher-quality fallback. Smart routing can route to cheaper variants first and fallback on confidence thresholds. We also recommend adjusting temperature (0.0-0.3 for clinical triage deterministic answers) and top_p to narrow sampling.
[06:30] Maria Lopez: Can we do sampling determinism for consistency across retries?
[06:34] Ben Cho: Yes — set temperature to near-zero and top_p to 1 or use deterministic decoding. Also use logprobs and filtering on the application side.
[06:45] Raj Patel: Show me a retry scenario in the demo?
[06:50] Ben Cho: I'll simulate a network drop. First, normal response. Then I'll kill the connection mid-stream and show client-side retry with idempotency key.
[07:00] [Ben runs a script that starts a chat, stream starts, then Ben cuts network]
[07:18] Ben Cho: Connection killed. On retry, I resend the same idempotency key. The Hosted API responds with a new completion; because the previous run was interrupted, the service treats it as fresh unless it had persisted state. In many cases you'd want to fetch the earlier partial via logs if enabled.
[07:40] Tom Nguyen: So we can't resume exactly but can re-run cheaply?
[07:44] Ben Cho: Correct — cost depends on how far the original run progressed. If original made it to 60 tokens, re-run will re-generate those tokens and you'll be billed for both unless dedup was possible. That's why short retry windows and idempotency patterns matter.
[08:00] Maria Lopez: You mentioned caching to avoid re-gen. How would that look?
[08:05] Ben Cho: Example flow: store canonicalized user prompt and partial completion in an application-level cache (Redis). On retry, check cache first — if you have a completed answer up to N tokens, return it. If missing tail only, call the model with prompt=prefix+missing_tail and stitch. For more advanced use we support prefix/KV cache server-side for repeated prefixes.
[08:30] Raj Patel: Can Redwood's Console show per-token billing to map cost back to features?
[08:36] Ben Cho: Yes, Console breaks costs down to input vs output tokens, model variant, and shows percentile latency. You can tag requests by route or API key for cost allocation.
[08:50] Maria Lopez: What about batching? If we need to push 80 rps can batching help us reduce cost?
[08:55] Ben Cho: Batching helps throughput on Dedicated and can reduce per-token overhead but adds latency. Continuous batching in Redwood groups requests for short windows; you can set SLO windows to control max batching latency. For your 200ms p95, batching window needs to be pretty tight, maybe 10-20ms to preserve p95.
[09:20] Tom Nguyen: Any quantization advice for Dedicated?
[09:24] Ben Cho: For Dedicated, quantized LLMs (4-bit/8-bit) give big cost improvements; Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization level per workload. For hosted we have pre-quantized variants that balance latency vs quality.
[09:40] Maria Lopez: Let's talk about a concrete pilot: what do you recommend we send you for the benchmark?
[09:45] Ben Cho: A representative prompt set (200-500 prompts), expected concurrency pattern (peak & base), and your SLOs. We'll run the benchmark against hosted and against a dedicated config to show tradeoffs.
[10:00] Raj Patel: We'll do that. One more technical: how do you handle streaming over websockets vs SSE? Latency differences?
[10:08] Ben Cho: Websockets have slightly lower overhead and are bi-directional; SSE is simpler but only server->client. For mobile clients, SSE sometimes easier because of proxies. We recommend websockets for low-latency, high-frequency interactions.
[10:26] Alice Morgan: Quick pause — any blockers on compliance side?
[10:29] Raj Patel: We need SOC2, infra diagram, and a rough contract for pilot — nothing else.
[10:34] Alice Morgan: Will send.
[10:36] [pause]
[10:45] Ben Cho: Ok back to a demo snippet: I'll show adjusting temperature and max_new_tokens and how the response changes.
[10:52] [Ben runs two requests side-by-side: temp=0.0 vs temp=0.8]
[11:10] Ben Cho: With temp=0.0 you see very deterministic phrasing; temp=0.8 more creative — for clinical triage we almost always use 0.0-0.2.
[11:26] Tom Nguyen: For multi-turn, how do we manage context window? We don't want to send full patient history every call.
[11:32] Ben Cho: Use summarization or store context in KV cache. Redwood also supports windowing policies: keep last N turns and a summary token that you update periodically. That reduces token size and cost.
[11:50] Maria Lopez: Any limits on token window for hosted?
[11:54] Ben Cho: Hosted supports up to 32k context on some variants; default medium is 8k. We'll surface exact limits per model in the model catalog.
[12:10] Raj Patel: You mentioned smart routing earlier — can we route by confidence?
[12:15] Ben Cho: Yes. You can set a policy: try small model, if response confidence (or logprob) below threshold, escalate to larger model synchronously or asynchronously. There's also automatic fallback in the platform that can route based on latency or cost budget.
[12:30] Maria Lopez: Show the console where we configure rollouts?
[12:33] Ben Cho: Sure — Console -> Deployments -> Rollouts. You can do canary % splits, A/B, or rule-based by request metadata (e.g., route critical customers to large model).
[12:50] [screen noise]
[13:10] Raj Patel: On the billing front, how granular is the metering?
[13:14] Alice Morgan: Down to token and model variant, and we can send daily usage exports to your billing system. For pilot we'll provide a simple estimate based on sample prompts.
[13:28] Tom Nguyen: Are there SDKs for streaming in Java/Go/Python?
[13:31] Ben Cho: Yes — SDKs for Python, Node, Java, and Go. They handle websocket reconnect and basic retry helpers. We also provide a sample harness for benching.
[13:45] Maria Lopez: Ok let's cover an edge case: partial hallucination halfway. If the model begins to hallucinate, can we abort quickly and fallback?
[13:53] Ben Cho: You can monitor token-level logprobs or use an assistant classifier. If you detect low confidence, you can abort and route to a deterministic variant or call a retrieval-augmented path (RAG). Redwood supports function-calling hooks and tooling to integrate retrieval before generation.
[14:12] Raj Patel: Good. Any notes about data residency? We operate in EU and US.
[14:17] Alice Morgan: Hosted has region pins; we can run in EU regions and do data residency controls. For strict residency we recommend Private with VPC.
[14:30] Maria Lopez: Let's wrap with next steps.
[14:33] Alice Morgan: Recap: we'll send pricing & pilot terms, SOC2 + infra diagram, Ben will share streaming docs and sample code, and you (Tom) will send prompt set and traffic trace. We'll schedule a benchmark run next week.
[14:49] Raj Patel: Sounds good. Anything else?
[14:52] Tom Nguyen: Maybe one final quick question: can we simulate mid-stream drop and get logs to correlate requests?
[14:58] Ben Cho: Yes — if you enable request logs and 30-day retention we can pull the partial traces. For pilot we'll enable 7-day logging and correlate by idempotency key.
[15:12] Maria Lopez: Thanks, that's helpful.
[15:15] Alice Morgan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and set up the benchmark.
[15:20] Raj Patel: Appreciate it.
